messages.author: c9c15d444d9b11d9
messages.subject: DO cross questions
parts:
We are looking for genetic modifiers of a gene knockout. The gene KO is on the X chromosome. We already know that KO/X[C57BL6/J] x males from 8 founder strains of DO yields F1 with heritable phenotypic variation. Now we are doing the DO cross to map the modifiers. Here is our current cross strategy: KO/X[C57BL6/J] x DO male -> F1 KO male. Genotype and phenotype the F1 males. 

Questions:
- In R/qtl2, what is the correct cross_type, and what should the cross_info file look like
- If we take the F1 KO/X females and cross to DO male, will this increase the statistical power or information yield of the cross? Could the data from the F1 cross and F2 cross be integrated in the same analysis?

Thank you.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: DO cross questions
parts:
You can use the cross type "dof1". There is some discussion of the input file information required at the following

    https://kbroman.org/qtl2/assets/vignettes/input_files.html#DOF1

The basic thing is that the parental genotype data needs 8 strains: the 8 DO founders, and then the strain the DO mice were crossed to. So C57BL6/J, repeated.

Regarding your idea of crossing pairs of these (KO x DO)F1 mice to make an F2, I think I would prefer to see many more (KO x DO)F1. Ultimately, you'll be as interested in mapping precision as in power, and getting additional F1s will provide more information in that regard.

cheers,
karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: DO cross questions
parts:
I feel like the F2 individuals are equally or maybe less informative than the F1 individuals. 
For power to detect a QTL, they are about equal, provided that the F2 cross is not just a few large sibships.

More importantly, for precision of mapping a QTL: the problem with the F2, is that they will be in sibships. Most of the mapping precision is coming from the recombination events on the DO chromosome, which accumulated over the many generations of the DO. But in the F2 mice, you’ll be seeing pieces of the same set of DO chromosomes repeatedly, and so the same historical recombination events repeated, whereas if you had a set of independent F1 mice, each would have different, independent sets of recombination events.

karl

messages.subject: Re: DO cross questions
parts:
I set crosstype="dof1"
I appended the C57bl6j genotype info to the end of each line of the file containing the DO founder strain genotypes. For example, the first several lines of chr1 is:
# Founder genotypes (A/B/-) for GigaMUGA chromosome 1
# nrow 8565
# ncol 10
marker,A,B,C,D,E,F,G,H,I
JAX00000010,A,A,B,B,A,B,B,A,A
JAX00000010r,A,A,B,B,A,B,B,A,A
UNCHS000003,A,A,A,A,A,B,B,B,A
JAX00240606,A,A,A,A,A,B,A,A,A
JAX00240613,B,B,A,A,B,A,A,B,B
JAX00240636,B,B,B,B,B,B,B,A,B
UNCHS000005,A,A,A,A,A,B,B,A,A

Trying to read this with read_cross2() yields this message:
founder_geno should have 9 founders (the CC founders plus the 9th strain to which the DO individuals were crossed)
and this warning:
3. In read_cross2("test.json") : length(alleles) [8] != expected number [8]
4: In check_cross2(output) : founder_geno has incorrect size on chr 1

It seems there is a problem with the founder_geno file. The file does have 9 strains but it seems that rqtl2 is not recognizing it properly. 
Many thanks.
Bill

Thank you so much. Apologize for the question caused by those errors in the two files. The corrected files load without a problem.

 

I went through the rest of the vignette on QC analysis of DO crosses (https://kbroman.org/qtl2/assets/vignettes/do_diagnostics.html). When I checked for percent genotyping errors, I got error rates of 30-35% for each individual. I wonder if this reflects my data quality, or if there is an issue with using these functions on this type of cross?

pr <- calc_genoprob(bths, error_prob=0.002, map_function="c-f")
e<-calc_errorlod(bths,pr)
e<-do.call("cbind",e)
head(errors_ind)

117447 117443 117446 117448 117444 117445
33.98384 33.06762 33.62928 33.47728 34.04905 33.74365

On the other hand, the missing genotype frequency was very low, perhaps suggesting that the data quality is ok.

percent_missing <- n_missing(bths, "ind", "prop")*100
head(percent_missing)

117447 117443 117446 117448 117444 117445
0.5298178 0.4155260 0.5085542 0.4934925 0.4731148 0.5307037
